nodes.statement_short: Leading term from the series remark; write $L^{p,+}=\sigma tAL^{p+1}$, use the double integral representation and bound $|\delta_m|$.

nodes.name: Cost of $\|Av_{m+1}\|_2$
nodes.statement: If the error estimate~\eqref{eresphijcor} is to be evaluated, the effort of the computation of $\|A v_{m+1}\|_2$ is comparable to one additional step of the \tjnew{Krylov} iteration.
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{Err}_1$ is an upper bound in the Hermitian case
nodes.statement: \tjnew{For the nonexpansive case} with $\sigma=1$ and \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(t)| = \delta_m(t) > 0 ~~~\text{for}~~t > 0. \end{equation*} This leads to the following upper bounds for the errors $L^p_m$ and $L^{p,+}_m$ with $p\geq 0$: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \|L^p_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \, t \, \underbrace{e_m^\ast \, \varphi_{p+1}(tT_m) \, e_1}_{\geq\, 0} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \,\tau_{m+1,m} \, t^2 \, \underbrace{e_m^\ast \, \varphi_{p+2}(tT_m) \, e_1}_{\geq\, 0}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
assumptions: \tjnew{For the nonexpansive case} with $\sigma=1$ and \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$
nodes.statement_short: For Hermitian $A$, $\sigma=1$: $\delta_m>0$, so $\mathrm{Err}_1$-type estimates are true upper bounds.
nodes.label: upperboundphi

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (Hermitian case)
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)={\rm e}^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sigma=1$. For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \mathbb R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} {\rm e}^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation} Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*} We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*} For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\varphi$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*} Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\mathrm{d} \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}. To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,A\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\varphi_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Mean value form shows the divided difference is positive; then the defect integral evaluates exactly to $\varphi$-function entries. Cases $p=0$, $p\ge1$ and corrected.

nodes.name: Hermite quadrature interpretation of the leading error term
nodes.statement: The term on the right-hand side of~\eqref{asy-leading} is a computable error estimate, which has been investigated more closely in Section~\ref{sec:theorypart}. It can also be interpreted in an alternative way. \wa{To this end we again proceed from the integral representation~\eqref{LDint}, \begin{equation} L_m(t)v = \int_0^t \underbrace{E(t-s)\,D_m(s)}_{=:\;\Theta_m(s,t)}v\,\mathrm{d} s. \end{equation} Due to $ \| D_m(t)v \| = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m-1}) $, \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\mathrm{d}^j}{\mathrm{d}\,s^j}\,D_m(s)v\big|_{s=0} = 0, \quad j=0,\ldots,m-2, \end{equation*} and the same is true for the integrand in~\eqref{LDint-1}, \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\partial^j}{\partial s^j}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\big|_{s=0} = 0, \quad j=0,\ldots,m-2. \end{equation*} Analogously as in~\cite{auzingeretal13a}, this allows us to approximate~\eqref{LDint-1} by \tjnew{a Hermite quadrature} formula in the form \begin{equation} \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s \approx \frac{t}{m}\,\Theta_m(t,t)v = \frac{t}{m}\,D_m(t)v. \end{equation} From~\eqref{Dm-lead}, \begin{equation*} \frac{t}{m}\,D_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\frac{(\sigma t)^{m}}{m!}\,v_{m+1} + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}), \end{equation*} which is the same as~\eqref{asy-leading}. This means that the quadrature approximation~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} approximates the leading error term in an asymptotically correct way.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: Approximating the defect integral by an order-$m$ Hermite quadrature $\frac{t}{m}D_m(t)v$ reproduces the leading error term.

nodes.name: Order of the Hermite quadrature error
nodes.statement: The quadrature error in~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} is $ {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) $.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: Proof of the quadrature error order
nodes.statement: It is useful to argue this also in a direct way: By construction, the Hermite quadrature formula underlying~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} is of order~$ m $, and its error has the Peano representation (cf. also~\cite{auzingeretal13a}) \begin{equation} \frac{t}{m}\,\Theta_m(t,t) - \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s = \int_0^t \frac{s\,(t-s)^{m-1}}{m!}\, \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s. \end{equation} Here, $ \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $, because $ \tfrac{\mathrm{d}^{m}}{\mathrm{d} s^{m}}\,D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $ which follows from $ D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(s^{m-1}) $. This shows that, indeed, the quadrature error~\eqref{quad-peano} is $ {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) $.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: Peano kernel representation of the order-$m$ Hermite quadrature error with an $O(1)$ $m$-th derivative.

nodes.name: Improved Hermite quadrature
nodes.statement: Furthermore, a quadrature formula of order $ m+1 $ can be constructed by including an additional evaluation of \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\partial}{\partial s}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\big|_{s=t} = D_m^{[2]}(t)v, \quad \text{with} \quad D_m^{[2]}(t) = \tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} D_m(t) - \sigma A\,D_m(t). \end{equation*} A routine calculation shows \begin{equation} \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s = \frac{2\,t}{m+1}\,D_m(t)v - \frac{t^2}{m(m+1)}\,D_m^{[2]}(t)v + {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+2}), \end{equation} where the error depends on $ \tfrac{\mathrm{d}^{m+1}}{\mathrm{d} s^{m+1}}\,D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: Adding the derivative $D_m^{[2]}$ of the defect gives an order-$(m+1)$ quadrature for the error integral.

nodes.name: Cheap evaluation of the defect derivative
nodes.statement: This may be considered as an improved error estimate\footnote{In the setting of~\cite{auzingeretal13a} (higher-order splitting methods) such an improved error estimate was not taken into account since it cannot be evaluated with reasonable effort in that context.} which can be evaluated using \begin{equation*} \tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} D_m(t)v = \sigma^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,e_m^\ast(T_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m})e_1 v_{m+1}. \end{equation*} With the solution in the Krylov subspace, ${\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} e_1$ with $e_m^\ast {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} e_1 = ({\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} e_1)_m$, we can compute the derivative of the defect at $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cost, \begin{align*} \tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} D_m(t)v &= \sigma^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,e_m^\ast(T_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m})e_1 v_{m+1} \\ &= \sigma^2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,\big((T_m)_{m,m}\, ({\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} e_1)_m + (T_m)_{m,m-1}\, ({\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} e_1)_{m-1}\big)v_{m+1}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: Positivity of $|\delta_m|$ near zero
nodes.statement: Let us denote $f(t):=|\delta_m(t)|$ and assume $f(t)>0$ in a sufficiently small interval $(0,T]$.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: effective order
nodes.statement: The effective order of the function $ f(t) $ can be understood as the slope of the double-logarithmic function \begin{align*} &\xi(\tau)=\ln(f({\rm e}^{\tau}))~~~\text{with}~~\tau=\ln t, \\ \text{with derivative} \quad &\xi'(\tau)=\frac{f'({\rm e}^{\tau})\,{\rm e}^{\tau}}{f({\rm e}^{\tau})}. \end{align*} We denote the order by \begin{equation} \rho(t)=\frac{f'(t)\,t}{f(t)}, \end{equation} and obtain \begin{equation*} f(t)=\frac{f'(t)\,t}{\rho(t)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: Effective order $\rho(t)=tf'(t)/f(t)$: the slope of $\ln f$ against $\ln t$.

nodes.name: Mean value form of the defect integral
nodes.statement: Integration and application of the mean value theorem shows the existence of $t^\ast\in[0,t]$ with \begin{equation*} \int_0^t f(s)\,\mathrm{d} s= \frac{1}{\rho(t^\ast)} \int_0^t f'(s)\,s\,\mathrm{d} s, \end{equation*} and integration by parts gives \begin{equation*} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \,\mathrm{d} s = \frac{t\, |\delta_m(t)|}{1+\rho(t^\ast)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: The defect integral equals $t|\delta_m(t)|/(1+\rho(t^\ast))$ for some $t^\ast\in[0,t]$.

nodes.name: Quadrature bounds on the defect integral
nodes.statement: With the plausible assumption that the order is bounded by $1\leq \tilde{m}\leq \rho(t) \leq m-1 =\rho(0+)$ for $t\in[0,T]$, we obtain \begin{equation} \tfrac{t}{m}\,|\delta_m(t)| \leq \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \,\mathrm{d} s \leq \tfrac{t}{\tilde{m}+1}\,|\delta_m(t)| \leq \tfrac{t}{2}\,|\delta_m(t)|. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
assumptions: the order is bounded by $1\leq \tilde{m}\leq \rho(t) \leq m-1 =\rho(0+)$ for $t\in[0,T]$
nodes.statement_short: Hermite quadrature underestimates and the trapezoidal rule overestimates the defect integral.

nodes.name: Trapezoidal estimate is an upper bound but not asymptotically correct
nodes.statement: The inequalities~\eqref{defintbounds} show that the error estimate based on the trapezoidal quadrature~\eqref{luquadtrapez} leads to an upper bound of the error. The error estimate based on Hermite quadrature \eqref{eq:hermitquadnorm} leads to a lower bound of the integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}, which not necessarily leads to a lower bound for the norm of the error. \tjnew{In contrast to~\eqref{eq:hermitquadnorm}, the error estimate~\eqref{luquadtrapez} is not asymptotically correct for $ t \to 0 $.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: effective order quadrature
nodes.statement: With $\rho(0+)=m-1$ and the assumptions that the effective order is slowly decreasing locally at $t=0$ and sufficiently smooth, we suggest choosing $\tilde{m}=\rho(t)$ for a step of size $t$ \tjnew{to} improve the quadrature based estimate. \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \, \mathrm{d} s \approx \tau_{m+1,m} \tfrac{t}{\rho(t)+1} \,|\delta_m(t)|, \end{equation} We will refer to this as \emph{effective order quadrature} estimate. In the limit $t\to0$ this choice of quadrature is equivalent to the Hermite quadrature and, therefore, asymptotically correct.
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\tilde m=\rho(t)$ to get the effective order quadrature estimate $\tau t|\delta_m(t)|/(\rho(t)+1)$, asymptotically correct.
nodes.label: remark:quadnew

nodes.name: Superlinear convergence onset
nodes.statement: We recall from~\cite{hoclub97} that superlinear convergence as a function of $ m $, the dimension of the underlying Krylov space, sets in for \begin{equation} t\, \|A\|_2 \lessapprox m. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
conclusions: superlinear convergence as a function of $ m $, the dimension of the underlying Krylov space, sets in for
nodes.statement_short: Superlinear convergence in $m$ sets in roughly for $t\|A\|_2\lesssim m$.

nodes.name: Restarted Krylov time propagation
nodes.statement: We split the time range $[0,t]$ into $N$ subintervals, \begin{align*} 0&=t_0<t_1<\ldots<t_N=t, \\ \text{with step sizes}~~\Delta t_j&= t_{j}-t_{j-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{align*} The exact solution at time $t_j$ is denoted by $ \mv{j} $, whence \begin{equation*} \mv{j} = E(\Delta t_{j})\mv{j-1}=E(t_{j})v,\quad\text{with}\quad \mv{0}=v. \end{equation*} For simplicity we assume that the dimension $m$ of the Krylov subspace is fixed over the substeps. We obtain approximations $ \mw{j }$ to $ \mv{j} $ by applying multiple restarted Krylov steps, with orthonormal bases $ V_m^{[j]} $ and upper Hessenberg matrices $ T_m^{[j]} $. Starting from $ \mw{0} = v $, for $ j=1,\ldots,N $, \begin{align*} \mw{j} := S_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_{j}) \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}} \big(V_m^{[j]}\big)^\ast \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}}e_1. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: Split $[0,t]$ into substeps and propagate by a fresh Krylov approximation $V^{[j]}_m e^{\sigma\Delta t_jT^{[j]}_m}e_1$ on each.

nodes.name: Accumulated error $L_m^\star(t)v$
nodes.statement: The error matrix in the $j$-th step is denoted by \begin{equation*} L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_{j}) := E(\Delta t_{j})-S_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_{j}), \end{equation*} and the accumulated error by \begin{equation} L_m^{\star}(t)v=\mv{N}-\mw{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.

nodes.name: Accumulated error representation
nodes.statement: With \begin{align*} \mv{j}-\mw{j} &= E(\Delta t_j)\mv{j-1}-S_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1} \\ &= E(\Delta t_j)(\mv{j-1}-\mw{j-1}) + L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1} \end{align*} we obtain \begin{equation*} L_m^{\star}(t)v = \sum_{j=1}^N E(\Delta t_N)\cdots E(\Delta t_{j+1})\,L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
conclusions: L_m^{\star}(t)v = \sum_{j=1}^N E(\Delta t_N)\cdots E(\Delta t_{j+1})\,L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1}.

nodes.name: Accumulated error bound
nodes.statement: Recall our premise that $E(\cdot)$ is \wa{nonexpansive} and assume that the local error is bounded by \begin{equation} \|L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j)\mw{j}\|_2 \leq {\rm tol} \cdot \Delta t_j. \end{equation} Then, \begin{equation*} \|L_m^{\star}(t)v\|_2 \leq \sum_{j=1}^N \|L_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_j) \mw{j-1}\|_2 \leq {\rm tol} \sum_{j=1}^N \Delta t_j = {\rm tol} \cdot t. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
assumptions: the local error is bounded by
nodes.statement_short: If each substep error is at most tol times its step size, the accumulated error is at most tol times $t$.

nodes.name: Step size control based on $\mathrm{Err}_a$
nodes.statement: For a single substep, the error estimate~\eqref{errornew} suggests a step size to satisfy a given error tolerance ${\rm tol}$ as \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{{\rm tol}\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/m},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation} For a local error as in~\eqref{localerror}, we replace ${\rm tol}$ by $ (\Delta t_j\,\,{\rm tol})$ in~\eqref{choosestepbyEra} and obtain \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{{\rm tol}\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/(m-1)},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: Invert $\mathrm{Err}_a$ to get the step size meeting the tolerance directly.

nodes.name: Heuristic step size control
nodes.statement: For a step, with step size $\Delta t_{j-1}$ and estimated error $\mathrm{Err}^{[j-1]}$, a reasonable size for the subsequent step can be chosen as \begin{equation} \Delta t_{j} = \left( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j}}\,\,{\rm tol}}{\mathrm{Err}^{[j-1]}}\right)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j-1},\quad j=2,\ldots,N. \end{equation} In~\eqref{heuristicstepsize} we only need the evaluation of the error estimate for the previously computed step with step size $\Delta t_{j-1}$, and we can substitute $\mathrm{Err}_1$ for $\mathrm{Err}^{[j-1]}$.
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
output: a reasonable size for the subsequent step
nodes.statement_short: Scale the previous step size by $(\Delta t\,\mathrm{tol}/\mathrm{Err})^{1/m}$ using the previous step's error estimate.

nodes.name: Step size iteration in the Hermitian case
nodes.statement: In the case of a Hermitian matrix $A$ the matrix $T_m$ is symmetric, tridiagonal and real-valued which allows cheap and robust computation of its eigenvalue decomposition. The eigenvalue decomposition of $T_m$ is independent of the step size $\Delta t$ and allows cheap evaluation of $\mathrm{Err}_1$ for multiple choices of $\Delta t$. In this case we can cheaply adapt the choice of $\Delta t_j$ in an iterative manner before continuing to time step $j+1$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta t_{j,1}&:= \Delta t_{j-1}~~\text{or result of~\eqref{choosestepbyEralocal}},\\ \Delta t_{j,l}&:= \Big( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j,l}}\,\,{\rm tol}}{\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}}\Big)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j,l-1},~~~~~ l=2,\ldots,N_j,\\ \Delta t_{j}&:=\Delta t_{j,N_j}.\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} By choosing $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ as an error estimate for the Krylov approximation of the $j$-th step with time step $\Delta t_{j,l-1}$. For $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ we can use $\mathrm{Err}_1$ or estimates given in Section~\ref{sec:defectquad}. The aim of the iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} is to determine a step size $\Delta t_{j,\infty}$ with $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,\infty]}={\rm tol}$. The convergence behavior of iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} depends on the structure of the corresponding error estimate. In our practical examples this iteration converges monotonically in a small number of steps. This step size iteration can also be used for the case of non-Hermitian $A$ with the drawback of higher computational cost for the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ for every $j$ and $l$.
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: For Hermitian $A$ the eigendecomposition of $T_m$ allows iterating the heuristic step size within a step until $\mathrm{Err}=\mathrm{tol}$.
nodes.label: reqmark:stepsizeiteration

nodes.name: Free Schr\"odinger equation
nodes.statement: We consider \begin{equation} H=\tfrac{1}{4}\, \text{tridiag}(-1,2,-1) \in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, \end{equation} with dimension $n=10\,000$. The matrix $H$ is \tjnew{associated with a finite difference or finite element discretization of the one-dimensional negative Laplacian}. With $A=H$ and $\sigma=-{\rm i}$, in~\eqref{exp(itA)v} we obtain the free Schr{\"o}dinger equation.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Discrete Hubbard model
nodes.statement: We consider the following Hubbard Hamiltonian, in second quantization and without chemical potential: \begin{equation} H=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j,\sigma} v_{ij} c_{j\sigma}^{\dagger} c_{i\sigma} + \sum_{j,\sigma} U \hat{n}_{j\sigma}\hat{n}_{j\sigma'}, \end{equation} where $i,j$ sum over the number of sites $n_{\text{sites}}$ and the spins $\sigma,\sigma' \in\{\uparrow,\downarrow \}$ where $\sigma'$ is the opposite spin to $\sigma$.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Numerical verification of the upper error bound
nodes.statement: We observe that the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_1$ is a good approximation \tjnew{to the error}, but it is not an upper bound in general. In contrast, $\mathrm{Err}_a$ is a \tjnew{proven} upper error bound. Up to round-off error, for $m=10$ we observe the correct asymptotic behavior of $\mathrm{Err}_a$ and $\mathrm{Err}_1$. For larger choices of $m$ the asymptotic regime starts at time steps for which the error is already close to round-off precision. Therefore, for larger choices of $m$, the Krylov approximation, as a time integrator, cannot achieve its full order for typical time steps in double precision.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Verification for $\varphi_1$ and corrected Krylov approximation
nodes.statement: We verify the error estimates in the skew-Hermitian setting of the free Schr{\"o}dinger equation~\eqref{Hschroe} for the standard Krylov approximation of the $\varphi_1$ function in Figure~\ref{fig:numexfreeSchrophi1} and the corrected Krylov approximation of the matrix exponential function in Figure~\ref{fig:numexfreeSchrocor}. In Figure~\ref{fig:numexfreeSchrophi1} the error estimator $\mathrm{Err}_1$ refers to formula~\eqref{LPnextphierrorest} and $\mathrm{Err}_a$ shows the \tjnew{upper error bound}~\eqref{eresphij} from Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}, both for the case $p=1$. In Figure~\ref{fig:numexfreeSchrocor}, $\mathrm{Err}_1$ is from formula~\eqref{LPplusnextphierrorest} and $\mathrm{Err}_a$ denotes the \tjnew{upper error bound}~\eqref{eresphijcor} from Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}, both for the case $p=0$.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Illustration of quadrature error estimates
nodes.statement: Figure~\ref{fig:num-quad2} refers to estimates based on the trapezoidal rule~\eqref{luquadtrapez}, the effective order quadrature according to Remark~\ref{remark:quadnew}, and the Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:hermitquadnorm}. For our test problems the assumptions from Section~\ref{sec:defectquad} on the defect and its effective order are satisfied for a significant range of values of~$ t $. We also observe that the inequalities~\eqref{defintbounds} are satisfied. The effective order and Hermite quadrature estimates behave in an asymptotically correct way, while the trapezoidal rule estimate leads to an upper \tjnew{error} bound which is not sharp for $t\to 0$.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Effective order formula (skew-Hermitian case)
nodes.statement: For the skew-Hermitian case $\sigma=-{\rm i}$ and $A=H$ we obtain \begin{align*} &|\delta_m(t)|= \big(({\rm e}^{{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_m({\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_m\big)^{1/2}~~~\text{and effective order $\rho(t)$, see~\eqref{def:effectiveorder},}\\ &\rho(t)=\frac{t\,\big(|\delta_m(t)|\big)'}{|\delta_m(t)|} = \frac{{\rm i}\,t\, (T_m)_{m-1,m}}{2}\bigg( \frac{({\rm e}^{{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_{m-1}}{({\rm e}^{{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_m} -\frac{({\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_{m-1}}{({\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_m}\bigg). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Mass conservation
nodes.statement: In exact arithmetic we obtain mass conservation for the skew-Hermitian case: For the case $\|v\|_2=1$ and standard Krylov approximation $S_m(t)v$ we have \begin{equation} \|S_m(t)v\|_2 = \|V_m {\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1\|_2 = e_1^\ast {\rm e}^{{\rm i}\,t\,T_m} V_m^\ast V_m{\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1=1. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Rounding of step sizes in Expokit
nodes.statement: In the Expokit code the step sizes are rounded to $2$ digits in every step. Rounding the step size can give too large errors in some steps. This makes it necessary to include safety parameters in Expokit which on the other hand slow down the performance of the code. It seems advisable to avoid any kind of rounding of step sizes.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Step size comparison on the Hubbard model
nodes.statement: In Table~\ref{table:stepsize10steps} we compare the total time step $t$ for the Krylov approximation with $m=10$ and $m=30$ after $N=10$ steps obtained with the different step size control strategies. For the local error we choose the tolerance ${\rm tol}=10^{-8}$. The original Expokit code seems to give larger step sizes, but it also uses a larger number of matrix-vector multiplications, see Remark~\ref{remark:cheapvsexpensive}. The error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a$ leads to optimal step sizes for $m=10$ and close to optimal step sizes for $m=30$. For any choice of $m$ the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a$ gives reliable step sizes. The trapezoidal quadrature rule overestimates the error and, therefore, step sizes are smaller. The effective order quadrature and $\mathrm{Err}_1$ give optimal step sizes. With the assumptions of Section~\ref{sec:defectquad} (which apply to our test examples), the trapezoidal and effective order quadrature give reliable step sizes. For the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_1$ we do not have results on the reliability of the step sizes since the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_1$ does not lead to an upper bound of the error \tjnew{in general}. The tested a priori estimates~\eqref{heuristicstepsize1},~\cite[Th. 4]{hoclub97}, and~\cite[(20)]{mohcar10} overestimate the error and lead to precautious step size choices. For all the tested versions the accumulated error $ L_m^{\star} $ (see~\eqref{Lmstar}) satisfies $\|L_m^{\star} v\|_2/t \leq {\rm tol}$.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement_short: With tol $=10^{-8}$, $\mathrm{Err}_a$-based step sizes are reliable and (near) optimal; a priori estimates are too cautious.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{Err}_a$ as a stopping criterion
nodes.statement: Apart from step size control, \tjnew{the upper error bound}~$\mathrm{Err}_a$ can be used on the fly to test if the dimension of the Krylov subspace is already sufficiently large to solve the problem in a single time step with the required accuracy.
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case

nodes.name: Cheap versus expensive error estimates
nodes.statement: Error estimates for the corrected Krylov approximation or improved error estimates such as the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} require additional matrix-vector multiplications. Instead of investing computational effort in improving the error estimate, one may as well increase the dimension of the standard Krylov subspace. For comparison we test the original Expokit code, the corrected Krylov approximation with error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a^+$ and the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} with Krylov subspace $m-1$. Table~\ref{Table:ExpensivErrEstvsCheapErrEst} shows that a standard Krylov approximation with dimension $m$ leads to better results, although all considered versions use the same number of matrix-vector multiplications. Since the reliability of error estimates such as $\mathrm{Err}_a$ has been demonstrated earlier, it appears that additional cost to improve the error estimate is not justified. \begin{table} \centering \caption{ All variants shown use exactly $m$ matrix-vector multiplications. Whereas Expokit, improved Hermite quadrature (i.H.quad) and $\mathrm{Err}_a^+$ imply higher cost for the error estimate, the other codes $\mathrm{Err}_a$, effective order quadrature (eff.o.quad) and $\mathrm{Err}_1$ use standard Krylov subspaces and do not spend additional matrix-vector multiplications on error estimates. } \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline m=10& \text{Expokit} & \mathrm{Err}_a^+ & \text{i.H.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_a & \text{eff.o.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_1 \\\hline t &0.6620&0.7828&0.5863&0.8346&0.8366&0.8368 \\ N & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 \\\hline \text{\#\,m-v} & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 \\\hline \|L_m^{\star} v\|_2/t & 4.1\cdot 10^{-09} & 8.8\cdot 10^{-09} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} & 9.8\cdot 10^{-09} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} \\\hline \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline m=30& \text{Expokit} & \mathrm{Err}_a^+ & \text{i.H.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_a & \text{eff.o.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_1 \\\hline t & 8.1900 & 9.5763 & 9.6591 & 9.7482 & 10.2378 & 10.2473 \\ N & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 \\\hline \text{\#\,m-v} & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 \\\hline \|L_m^{\star} v\|_2/t & 3.6\cdot 10^{-10} & 2.7\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.2\cdot 10^{-09} & 2.6\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.5\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.7\cdot 10^{-09} \\\hline \end{array} \end{aligned} \end{equation*} \end{table}
nodes.section: 8.1 The skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement_short: Extra matrix-vector products are better spent on a larger standard Krylov space than on improved error estimates.
nodes.label: remark:cheapvsexpensive

nodes.name: Heat equation
nodes.statement: For the heat equation, $H$ given in~\eqref{Hschroe}, we can also verify the error estimates, see Figure~\ref{fig:numexheat}. In comparison to the skew-Hermitian case we do not observe a large time regime for which the error is of the asymptotic order $m$. As shown in Proposition~\ref{upperboundphi} we do obtain \tjnew{an upper error bound} using $\mathrm{Err}_1$ for the heat equation. However, the evolution is not unitary but nonexpansive in this case, whence the asymptotics are not observed as clearly here.
nodes.section: 8.2 The Hermitian case

nodes.name: Effective order formula (Hermitian case)
nodes.statement: For the Hermitian case results of Proposition~\ref{upperboundphi} can be applied to obtain \begin{align*} &|\delta_m(t)| = \delta_m(t) = ({\rm e}^{{\rm i}\,t\,T_m}e_1)_m~~~\text{and effective order $\rho(t)$, see~\eqref{def:effectiveorder},}\\ &\rho(t)=\frac{t\,\big(|\delta_m(t)|\big)'}{|\delta_m(t)|} = t\,\bigg( \frac{(T_m)_{m,m-1}\,({\rm e}^{t\,T_m}e_1)_{m-1}}{({\rm e}^{t\,T_m}e_1)_m} + (T_m)_{m,m}\bigg). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 8.2 The Hermitian case

nodes.name: Convection-diffusion problem
nodes.statement: For a more general case we consider a convection-diffusion equation (see \cite{MN01,EE06}). \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\partial_t u = \Delta u - \tau_1 \partial_{x_1} u - \tau_2 \partial_{x_2} u,~~\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathbb R,~~~u=u(t,x),~~t\geq 0,~~ x\in\Omega=[0,1]^3,\\ &u(0,x)=v(x)~~\text{for}~x\in\Omega,~~u(t,x)=0~~\text{for}~x\in\partial\Omega. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Following \cite{MN01,EE06} we use a central finite difference scheme to discretize the partial differential operator in~\eqref{convdifpde}. The grid is chosen uniformly with $(n+2)^3$ points and mesh width $h=1/(n+1)$. The dimension $N$ of the discrete operator is $N=n^3$. Choosing $n=15$ we obtain $N=3357$. The discretized operator is given by \begin{align} &A=( I_{n\times n} \otimes (I_{n\times n} \otimes C_1) ) + ( B \otimes I_{n\times n} + I_{n\times n}\otimes C_2 ) \otimes I_{n\times n} )\in\mathbb R^{N\times N},~~~\text{with}\\ &~~~B=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1,-2,1)\in\mathbb R^n,~~~ C_i=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1+\mu_i,-2,1-\mu_i)\in\mathbb R^n,~~i=1,2,\notag \end{align} and $\mu_i=\tau_i\,(h/2)$. The spectrum of the non-normal matrix $A$ in~\eqref{Aconvdif} (see \cite{MN01}) satisfies \begin{align*} \text{spec}(A)\subseteq &\tfrac{1}{h^2}\,[-6-2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Re}(\theta),-6+2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Re}(\theta)] \\ &~\times \tfrac{1}{h^2}\,{\rm i}\,[-2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Im}(\theta),2\cos(\pi\,h)\text{Im}(\theta)] . \end{align*} with $\theta = 1 + \sqrt{1-\mu_1^2} + \sqrt{1-\mu_2^2}$. Therefore, the eigenvalues are complex-valued if at least one $\mu_i>1$. The matrix $A$ depends on the parameters $\mu_i$, correspondingly $\tau_i$, for which we consider two different cases, \begin{equation} \text{$\mu_1=0.9$, $\mu_2=1.1$},~~~\text{with}~~\text{spec}(h^2\,A) \subseteq [-9,-3] \times {\rm i}[-1,1], \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \text{$\mu_1=\mu_2=10$},~~~\text{with}~~\text{spec}(h^2\,A) \subseteq [-8,-4] \times {\rm i} [ -39,39]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 8.3 A non-normal problem

nodes.name: Error bounds for the non-normal problem
nodes.statement: The error estimates $\mathrm{Err}_a$ and $\mathrm{Err}_1$ are compared to the exact error norm $\|L_m(t) v\|_2$ in Figure~\ref{fig:numexcd0911} for the case~\eqref{cdsetting1} and in Figure~\ref{fig:numexcd1010} for the case~\eqref{cdsetting2}. As shown in Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a$ constitutes an upper error bound. The error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_1$ gives a good approximation of the error but has not been proven to give an upper bound in general. Compared to~\eqref{cdsetting2}, the spectrum for~\eqref{cdsetting1} is closer to the Hermitian case. The spectrum for~\eqref{cdsetting2}, on the other hand, is dominated by large imaginary parts similarly as in the skew-Hermitian case. In Figure~\ref{fig:numexcd0911} we observe effects similar to the Hermitian case. The asymptotic order $m$ of the error does not hold for a large time regime, and the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a$ is not as sharp as in the skew-Hermitian case. On the other hand, in Figure~\ref{fig:numexcd1010}, we observe that the performance of the error estimates is closer to the skew-Hermitian case. Therefore, the upper error bound $\mathrm{Err}_a$ is sharp for a larger range of time steps. As already observed for the Hermitian and skew-Hermitian cases, the error of the Krylov approximation is closer to its asymptotic order $m$ for smaller choices of $m$.
nodes.section: 8.3 A non-normal problem

nodes.name: Taylor-expand the error to order $m$
nodes.statement: Taylor expansion. Due to $ L_m(t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(t^m) $, \tjnew{see~\eqref{orderofDmLm},} \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &L_m(t)v = E(t)v - S_m(t)v = \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m}{{m!}}(A^m v - V_m T_m^m\,e_1) + R_{m+1}(t),\\ &\text{with Taylor remainder}~~ R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Taylor-expand the error to order $m$

nodes.name: Use the Krylov identity to identify $A^mv - V_mT_m^me_1$ and conclude
nodes.statement: Multiplying the identity~\tjnew{{\eqref{HVTm}} (with $ j = m-1 $) by $ A $} and using~\eqref{krylovidentity} gives \begin{align*} A^m\,v &= A\,V_m T_m^{m-1} e_1 = (V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1} e_m^\ast) T_m^{m-1} e_1 \\ &= V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m}\, (e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1)\,v_{m+1} = V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m v_{m+1}, \end{align*} whence~\eqref{prop-3-proof} simplifies to~\eqref{asy-leading}. \qed
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Use the Krylov identity to identify $A^mv - V_mT_m^me_1$ and conclude

nodes.name: Write the interpolant in Newton form
nodes.statement: We proceed from the Newton representation of the interpolant $p_t(\lambda) $ from~\eqref{pt}, \begin{equation*} p_t(\lambda) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t}\,\omega_j(\lambda), \end{equation*} with $ \omega_j(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1) \cdots (\lambda-\lambda_{j}) $.
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Write the interpolant in Newton form

nodes.name: Evaluate $e_m^\ast\omega_j(T_m)e_1$
nodes.statement: {From~\eqref{eTe} and by definition of $ \gamma_m $, it is obvious that the $ \omega_j $ satisfy} \begin{equation*} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)\,e_1 = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & j=0,\ldots,m-2, \\ \gamma_m,& j=m-1. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $e_m^\ast\omega_j(T_m)e_1$

nodes.name: Derive the divided-difference identity for $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: Together with~\eqref{pt} this shows that the identity claimed in~\eqref{deltam-repr} is valid: \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}\,e_1 = e_m^\ast\,p_t(T_m) e_1 = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)e_1 = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Derive the divided-difference identity for $\delta_m$

nodes.name: Bound the divided difference by the derivative (Higham B.28)
nodes.statement: According to~\cite[(B.28)]{higham08} the divided difference can be estimated by \begin{align*} &|f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]| \leq \frac{\max_{z \in \Omega} D^{(m-1)}f_t(z)}{(m-1)!}\\ &\text{for convex $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb C$ which contains all eigenvalues $ \lambda_j$.} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the divided difference by the derivative (Higham B.28)

nodes.name: Use $\mathrm{Re}(\sigma\lambda_j)\le 0$ to get the bound
nodes.statement: With $D^{(m-1)}f_t(\lambda) = (\sigma\,t)^{m-1} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\lambda} $, $ |\sigma|=1 $ and $\text{Re}(\sigma \lambda_j)\leq 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}| \leq \frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}, \end{equation*} which implies the estimate~\eqref{deltam-repr} for $ \delta_m(t) $. \qed
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Use $\mathrm{Re}(\sigma\lambda_j)\le 0$ to get the bound

nodes.name: Start from the defect integral and apply the divided-difference bound
nodes.statement: We proceed from~\eqref{errestintdefect}.
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Start from the defect integral and apply the divided-difference bound

nodes.name: Integrate the bound on $|\delta_m|$
nodes.statement: For $ \delta_m $ defined in~\eqref{defdelta}, Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} implies \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(s)| \leq \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \gamma_m, \end{equation*} and this gives an upper bound for the error integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \int_0^t \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m \frac{t^{m}}{m!}, \end{equation*} which completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the bound on $|\delta_m|$

nodes.name: Justify the spectral assumption via the nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case ($ W(\sigma A) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $) which implies the requirement $ \text{spec}(\sigma T_m) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $, see~\eqref{subsetofspectrum}.} \qed
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Justify the spectral assumption via the nonexpansive case

nodes.name: Case $p=0$ follows from earlier results; assume $p\ge1$
nodes.statement: For $p=0$ the result directly follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:prop3},~\ref{prop:prop4} and Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp}. We now assume $ p \geq 1 $.
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Case $p=0$ follows from earlier results; assume $p\ge1$

nodes.name: Leading term via series representation
nodes.statement: Via the series representation~\eqref{defphiseries} of $\varphi_p$ we can determine the leading term of the error in an analogous way as in Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}: \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m \,(A^m v - V_m T_m^m e_1)}{(m+p)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}) \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sigma\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}), \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{leadingtermphij}.
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Leading term via series representation

nodes.name: Integral representation in terms of $L_m(\theta t)v$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, proceeding from~\eqref{defphiint} we obtain \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t A} v - V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t T_m} e_1 \big) \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta, \end{align*} with the error $L_m(t)v$ for the matrix exponential case.
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Integral representation in terms of $L_m(\theta t)v$

nodes.name: Apply the exponential bound and evaluate the Beta integral
nodes.statement: Now we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} to obtain \begin{align*} \| \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 \|_2 &\leq \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{(p-1)!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^m \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphij}. \qed
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the exponential bound and evaluate the Beta integral

nodes.name: Leading term from the asymptotics of $\varphi$ entries
nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{em-phi-e1} (with $j=p+2$) to~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} shows~\eqref{leadingtermphijcor}: \begin{equation*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\, \gamma_m\, \frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \,A v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Leading term from the asymptotics of $\varphi$ entries

nodes.name: Relate $L^{p,+}_m$ to $L^{p+1}_m$
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{prop:generalSaadsum} we observe \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \sigma\,t\,A \,\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Relate $L^{p,+}_m$ to $L^{p+1}_m$

nodes.name: Double integral representation via the defect
nodes.statement: Using the integral representation analogously as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi} for $L^{p+1}_m(t)v$ and formula~\eqref{LDint} for $L_m(t)v$, we obtain \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v &= \sigma\,t\,A\,\, L^{p+1}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} A\, L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} {\rm e}^{\sigma (\theta t-s) A} A v_{m+1} \delta_m( s)\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Double integral representation via the defect

nodes.name: Bound with $|\delta_m|$ estimate and evaluate the integral
nodes.statement: With norm inequalities \tjnew{(note the nonexpansive case)} and Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we obtain \begin{align*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \,t\,\|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m\, t^{m+1}\,\frac{1}{p!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta ^m\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphijcor}. \tjnew{Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case, see also the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:upperboundexp}.}\hfill\qed
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Bound with $|\delta_m|$ estimate and evaluate the integral

nodes.name: Lanczos gives real symmetric tridiagonal $T_m$ with distinct real eigenvalues
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}.
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Lanczos gives real symmetric tridiagonal $T_m$ with distinct real eigenvalues

nodes.name: Divided-difference representation of $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)={\rm e}^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sigma=1$.
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Divided-difference representation of $\delta_m$

nodes.name: Mean value form of the divided difference
nodes.statement: For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \mathbb R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} {\rm e}^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Mean value form of the divided difference

nodes.name: Conclude $\delta_m(t)>0$
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\delta_m(t)>0$

nodes.name: Case $p=0$: integrate $\delta_m$ exactly to a $\varphi_1$ entry
nodes.statement: We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Case $p=0$: integrate $\delta_m$ exactly to a $\varphi_1$ entry

nodes.name: Case $p\ge1$: integrate the $p=0$ bound against the $\varphi_p$ kernel
nodes.statement: For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\varphi$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*} Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\mathrm{d} \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}.
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Case $p\ge1$: integrate the $p=0$ bound against the $\varphi_p$ kernel

nodes.name: Corrected case by the same integral evaluation
nodes.statement: To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,A\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\varphi_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.
nodes.statement_short: Corrected case by the same integral evaluation

nodes.name: Split $[0,t]$ into $N$ substeps
nodes.statement: We split the time range $[0,t]$ into $N$ subintervals, \begin{align*} 0&=t_0<t_1<\ldots<t_N=t, \\ \text{with step sizes}~~\Delta t_j&= t_{j}-t_{j-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: Split $[0,t]$ into $N$ substeps

nodes.name: For each substep, propagate with a new Krylov approximation
nodes.statement: Starting from $ \mw{0} = v $, for $ j=1,\ldots,N $, \begin{align*} \mw{j} := S_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_{j}) \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}} \big(V_m^{[j]}\big)^\ast \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}}e_1. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: For each substep, propagate with a new Krylov approximation

nodes.name: Step size from $\mathrm{Err}_a$ for an absolute tolerance
nodes.statement: For a single substep, the error estimate~\eqref{errornew} suggests a step size to satisfy a given error tolerance ${\rm tol}$ as \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{{\rm tol}\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/m},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: Step size from $\mathrm{Err}_a$ for an absolute tolerance

nodes.name: Step size for error per unit step
nodes.statement: For a local error as in~\eqref{localerror}, we replace ${\rm tol}$ by $ (\Delta t_j\,\,{\rm tol})$ in~\eqref{choosestepbyEra} and obtain \begin{equation} \Delta t_j = \left(\frac{{\rm tol}\, \, m!}{\tau^{[j]}_{m+1,m}\gamma^{[j]}_m}\right)^{1/(m-1)},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7 The matrix exponential as a time integrator.
nodes.statement_short: Step size for error per unit step
